work: "Does the New Testament Call Jesus God?", Theological Studies 26 (1965)
edition: Theological Studies 26 (1965) pp. 545-573 (journal issue; PDF from theologicalstudies.net)
quote_orig: The question that forms the title of this article must be answered in the affirmative. In three clear instances and in five instances that have a certain probability Jesus is called God in the New Testament.
context_before: Brown states at the outset that he will not treat whether Jesus was God, since Nicaea settled that; the article asks what the New Testament says. The sentence opens the evaluation after he has reviewed the texts.
what_it_says: Brown answers his own title question 'yes': three clear and five probable NT instances call Jesus God.
claim_supported: (B) the NT writers portray Jesus as sharing YHWH's unique identity (title 'God' used of Jesus)
scholar_qualification: SUPPORTS US (on the NT texts, not on Jesus' own words). Brown says the affirmative answer concerns NT writers' usage; he explicitly says Jesus is never called God in the Synoptics and the Acts sermons do not call him God (see J8-07 and J8-11). Footnote 49 (not quoted) says the five 'probable' instances are less certain than the three.

chapter_or_section: Section 'Evaluation of the Evidence' (discussion of kyrios)
quote_orig: "Jesus is Lord" was evidently a popular confessional formula in New Testament times, and in this formula Christians gave Jesus the title kyrios which was the standard LXX translation for YHWH.
context_before: Brown argues that the use of 'God' (theos) for Jesus in the early second century continued a usage already begun in NT times, and that the confessional formula 'Jesus is Lord' is the starting point.
what_it_says: In 'Jesus is Lord' the title kyrios, the standard Septuagint rendering of YHWH, was given to Jesus, and so theos could also be applied to him.
claim_supported: (B) the NT writers portray Jesus as sharing YHWH's unique identity
scholar_qualification: SUPPORTS US, and it answers the video's gloss that 'kyrios' just means lord/master. Brown does not say kyrios always translates YHWH consciously: he writes that 'we do not assume that every time kyrios appears, it is used consciously as a translation of YHWH' (note 80, p. 566 n.). This is his only verified statement on the kyrios issue in the 1965 text.

work: "Does the New Testament Call Jesus God?", Theological Studies 26 (1965)

chapter_or_section: Section 'Texts Where the Use of the Title God for Jesus Is Dubious/Probable' (John)
quote_orig: More than the other Gospels, John brings the "God problem" to the fore in the ministry of Jesus (5:18; 7:58-59; 10:30-33); this is part of the Johannine technique of spelling out the challenge that Jesus brings to men, and of making explicit what was implicit in Jesus' ministry. Yet, John does show a certain caution about anachronism and so even in 10:33 ff. Jesus does not give a clear affirmation to the charge of the Jews that he is making himself God.
context_before: Brown moves from the Synoptics to John, where the charge of 'making himself God' appears.
what_it_says: John puts the 'God problem' at the centre of Jesus' ministry (5:18, 7:58-59, 10:30-33), but even in 10:33 Jesus does not clearly affirm the charge.
claim_supported: (A) Jesus himself speaks or acts as YHWH / claims divine identity (Brown's answer is: implicitly, not by explicit affirmation)
scholar_qualification: MIXED. For the video: Brown denies that Jesus gives a 'clear affirmation' in Jn 10:33. For us: Brown says John makes explicit what was implicit in Jesus' ministry and that the charge (making himself God) is what the Jews understood. The quote alone does not show Brown denies an implicit claim; he says the opposite about implicitness.
limits: Read in full from the journal's open PDF (theologicalstudies.net, Theological Studies 26 (1965) 545-573); printed page confirmed by running header; footnote numbers removed. Footnote markers removed. Brown's 1966 AB commentary on 10:30-33 is not read directly.

work: "Does the New Testament Call Jesus God?", Theological Studies 26 (1965)
edition: Theological Studies 26 (1965) pp. 545-573 (journal issue; PDF from theologicalstudies.net)
chapter_or_section: Section 'Evaluation of the Evidence' (Synoptics, Acts, earliest layers)
quote_orig: Even the fourth Gospel never portrays Jesus as saying specifically that he is God. The sermons which Acts attributes to the beginning of the Christian mission do not speak of Jesus as God. Thus, there is no reason to think that Jesus was called God in the earliest layers of New Testament tradition.
context_before: Brown has just said that Jesus is never called God in the Synoptic Gospels and that Mk 10:18 seems to preclude Jesus using the title of himself.
what_it_says: Brown's negative conclusion: no explicit 'God' self-designation by Jesus, and no 'God' title for Jesus in the earliest NT layers.
claim_supported: (A) Jesus himself speaks or acts as YHWH / claims divine identity (negative: explicit title, not implicit claim)
scholar_qualification: SUPPORTS THE VIDEO on the explicit title 'God' only. Brown's own words: 'saying specifically that he is God'. He does NOT say Jesus made no implicit claim to divine identity; he says in the same article that John makes explicit what was implicit (see J8-03). Use this to show the video's claim is narrower than Brown's.

quote_orig: Jn 20:28 portrays Jesus being confessed as God one week after the Resurrection. context_before: Brown treats the Thomas confession as a probable case of God-language for Jesus, and then raises a critical question about its setting.
what_it_says: Brown says John 20:28 is a confession of Jesus as God, but suspects it may be the evangelist's own confession placed on Thomas.
claim_supported: (B) and (C): Gospel writers portray Jesus as God / early confession (with critical doubt on the setting)
scholar_qualification: MIXED. Brown counts John 20:28 among the 'clear' instances in the same article (J8-01), but on this verse he says a critical reader would suspect the setting is the evangelist's own time, not Thomas' words. Brown's 1994 book says Thomas' 'My Lord and my God' is discussed on pp. 188-89 (see J8-08).

work: "Does the New Testament Call Jesus God?", Theological Studies 26 (1965)
edition: Theological Studies 26 (1965) pp. 545-573 (journal issue; PDF from theologicalstudies.net)
chapter_or_section: Section 'Texts That Seem to Imply the Title God Was Not Used' (Acts, earliest layers)
quote_orig: The sermons which Acts attributes to the beginning of the Christian mission do not speak of Jesus as God. Thus, there is no reason to think that Jesus was called God in the earliest layers of New Testament tradition. This negative conclusion is substantiated by the fact that Paul does not use the title in any epistle written before 58.
context_before: Brown closes the Gospel and Acts survey before turning to the Pauline letters.
what_it_says: Brown: no sign that Jesus was called God in the earliest NT layers; Paul does not use 'God' of Jesus before 58.
claim_supported: (E) chronology of the title 'God' for Jesus (a limit on early high Christology, not on implicit claims)
scholar_qualification: SUPPORTS THE VIDEO on the timing of the explicit title; it is a claim about when the title 'God' appears in the NT, not about Jesus' self-understanding. Brown then states the title appears later (Heb 1:8-9, John) and is 'frequent only toward the end of the period' (p. 567).
